text:
Preamble
The Malaysia - United Nations Sustainable Development Goals Framework (UNSDGF) for the period 2018-2020, titled “Prosperous, Inclusive and Resilient Futures,” describes the joint work of participating United Nations (UN) Agencies, Funds and Programmes (hereafter ‘UN Agencies’) of the UN Country Team (UNCT) in support of Malaysia’s attainment of the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development and the related Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). The UNSDGF also supports Malaysia’s transformation into a high-income and advanced nation. 
In this regard, the UNSDGF provides the collective strategic response of the UNCT to both new and remaining challenges of a nation on an accelerated development trajectory, building upon the vibrant and consistent progress Malaysia has made since its independence in 1957. It aligns the collaborative work of participating UN Agencies with Malaysia’s Vision 2020 and the Eleventh Malaysia Plan 2016-2020, while also underpinning the nation’s increasingly active role in the region and the wider international community.   In all, the Framework represents the shared view of the UNCT and the Government on areas that can benefit from a cohesive and joint strategic contribution of the UN System.
This is thus a dynamic and strategic agenda, driven by national priorities and international commitments, with the aim of being responsive to the of the Malaysian people. It is designed to be at the outcome level, to afford the flexibility and agility that would be necessary to respond effectively to the evolving needs of the Government and its people. The Framework takes a participatory and inclusive approach with a wide spectrum of stakeholders from around the country, namely, civil society, non-Government organizations, academia, think tanks, multilateral development institutions, the private sector, workers and employers, children, youth, and the general public, including women, to help address gaps and challenges at national and sub-national levels. In particular, it works to achieve the Agenda 2030/SDG goal of leaving no one behind, especially those currently furthest behind, and reach international standards and norms that would define a nation as fully developed.  It also will contribute to the work of the participatory and multi-stakeholder SDG governance structure that has been established by the Government for implementation, monitoring, evaluation and reporting on the 2030 Agenda, in which the different UN Agencies are actively engaged. 
SIGNATURES 
The Government of Malaysia, along with participating Agencies of the UNCT, comprising resident as well as non-resident UN Agencies, commit to working together under the UNSDGF 2018-2020 to support Malaysia’s transformation  by securing for its people a future that is inclusive, sustainable and resilient; that assures the well-being and a good quality of life of its citizens and others within its jurisdiction; and that is grounded in active citizen participation, transparency and accountability. As highlighted above, all these objectives are in line with Agenda 2030 and the SDGs, as well as with  the Eleventh Malaysia Plan.

We, the members of the United Nations Country Team in Malaysia, pledge our commitment, under the leadership of the Resident Coordinator, to foster cohesiveness and coherence among our agencies and to bring the combined experience and expertise, as well as the impartiality, values, global knowledge base and best practices of the UN System, to enhance the performance and impact of the work of the UNCT in Malaysia under the UNSDGF 2018-2020. This will be achieved by undertaking complementary, joint and coordinated activities, taking into account our individual Country Programmes, and guided by Agenda 2030 and the SDGs, as well as principles of the Charter of the United Nations and our Agency mandates thereof.

Executive Summary
The UN Agencies committed to this UNSDGF, under the leadership of the United Nations Resident Coordinator as head of the UNCT and the designated representative of the UN Secretary-General, consist of:
(a) Resident agencies, i.e., 1) UN Development Programme (UNDP), 2) UN Population Fund (UNFPA), 3) Office of the UN High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR), 4) UN Children’s Fund (UNICEF), 5) UN University-International Institute for Global Health (UNU-IIGH), 6) World Food Programme–UN Humanitarian Response Depot (WFP-UNHRD), 7) World Health Organization (WHO), 8) International Organization for Migration (IOM); and
(b) Non-resident agencies (operating from their regional headquarters in Bangkok, Jakarta or Vienna) i.e., 9) International Labour Organization (ILO), 10) Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights (OHCHR), 11) Joint UN Programme on HIV/AIDS (UNAIDS), 12) UN Entity for Gender Equality and the Empowerment of Women (UN Women), 13) UN Environment Programme (UNEP), 14) UN Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (UNESCO), 15) UN Industrial Development Organization (UNIDO),  16) International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA), and 17) United Nations Innovation Lab (UNTIL).
While UN Agencies with operational activities for development have Agency-specific Country Programmes with their relevant Government counterparts or line Ministries, the UNSDGF is the first overarching framework of the UN System in Malaysia that brings together the collective strengths of the various UN Funds, Programmes and specialised Agencies to deliver coordinated joint support in response to national priorities. It does not, however, impinge upon existing mechanisms and agreements between individual UN Agencies and their Government counterparts. 
Malaysia’s SDG implementation is divided into three phases. In the current Phase 1 (2016-2020), the Eleventh Malaysia Plan – premised on the theme “Anchoring Growth on People” – is the vehicle through which Malaysia will implement Agenda 2030 and the SDGs. . To a large extent, the Eleventh Malaysia Plan is in sync with the SDGs, working toward Malaysia becoming an advanced economy and inclusive nation in line with the aspirations of its Vision 2020. The Plan’s six strategic thrusts are aimed to address the ‘end-to-end’ needs of the rakyat (people) and the nation, while its six ‘game changers’ are innovative approaches to accelerate Malaysia’s development and growth. The SDGs have been further localized and mainstreamed through the National SDG Framework, which is a key guidance document for the UNSDGF. 
The outcome areas of this UNSDGF have been formulated in alignment with not only the Eleventh Malaysia Plan, but also the National SDG Roadmap for Phase 1, Malaysia’s Voluntary National Review to the 2017 High-Level Political Forum, the Regional Roadmap for Implementing the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development in Asia and the Pacific (Regional A-P 2030 Roadmap), and key priorities  outlined in the Report of the UN Secretary-General on Repositioning the UN Development System to Deliver on the 2030 Agenda. Based on these, the outcomes also are tailored to the comparative advantages, technical resources and work of the different UN Agencies that can be collectively brought to bear in the country to facilitate better coordination, communication, governance and partnership management.  The UNSDGF will be operationalised through a Results Matrix to be developed pursuant to the signing of this document.
Under the UNSDGF, the scope of work of the UNCT will be guided by national laws, rules, regulations and policies, as well as on-the-ground realities and circumstances, while also taking into account international law, treaties and instruments2 to which Malaysia is a State Party or has registered reservations to, as well as those that Malaysia has yet to ratify. 
Overall, this first common strategic framework of the UN System in Malaysia broadens options where results can be achieved through a more coherent, cohesive response by the UNCT, capitalising on its combined strengths and diverse expertise as Malaysia strives to achieve its next phase of development in a sustainable, resilient and inclusive manner. The Framework also is aimed at supporting Malaysia’s regional and international engagement vis-à-vis its contribution to peace and security, humanitarian response and the global partnership for development. 
The following are the four (4) key outcome areas that will be the focus of the joint work of participating UN Agencies under the UNSDGF 2018-2020:
Outcome Area 1: 	Effective Mainstreaming, Localisation, Monitoring Toward Achievement of the SDGs
Outcome Area 2: 	Enhanced Inclusivity, Empowerment of Women and Improved Well-Being for All Toward Leaving No One Behind (LNOB)
Outcome Area 3: 	Inclusive Governance and Human Rights for All
Outcome Area 4: 	Sustainable Economic Development, Prioritising Protection of the Environment and Natural Resources Management
1.0 Introduction
Malaysia is a nation of 31.4 million people of diverse ethnicities, faiths and cultures.  Strategically located in Southeast Asia, it is often regarded as a window to Asia as a whole. Malaysia has made significant progress since its independence in 1957 and is today an upper-middle-income country that ranks 59th out of 188 countries and territories in UNDP’s 2015 Human Development Index (HDI). Its HDI value of 0.789represents a 22.8 percent increase from its human development value in 1990. The country is a federation of states, and the form of government practiced is that of a parliamentary democracy with a constitutional monarchy.
Malaysia’s role in multilateralism, international cooperation and contributions to regional and international development are expected to evolve and become even more considerable as it transitions to Net Contributor Country (NCC) and fully developed status. Already, Malaysia (1) is a significant contributor to South-South Cooperation through the Malaysian Technical Corporation Programme, under the purview of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs; (2) is an influential voice on moderation through the Global Movement of Moderates Foundation; (3) has served on the UN Security Council for the 1964-1965, 1989-1990, 1999-2000 and 2015-2016 sessions, as well as on the Human Rights Council and several UN governing bodies; and (4) is an active facilitator of peace talks in the region, such as in the 2012 Framework Agreement on the Bangsamoro in Philippines, along with in southern Thailand. 
The country therefore has immense potential to contribute substantively to the global partnership for development, peace and security, through strategic partnerships with non-Government organisations and the private sector, and via bilateral and multilateral means. Malaysia also can influence cross-border linkages and partnerships through the ASEAN agenda for development and economic cooperation, thereby bringing about significant change that is critical in moving the 2030 Agenda forward.
1.1 Malaysia’s Longstanding and Growing Relationship with the UN System 
Malaysia has had a long and significant relationship with the United Nations (UN) System both in-country and internationally, through the many Funds, Programmes and specialised Agencies of the UN. It also has enjoyed active engagement with the high-level and policymaking organs of the UN as the world’s largest multilateral platform. This 60-year relationship has evolved in its myriad dimensions in parallel with the country’s development. The UN System began its partnership with Malaysia (then known as Malaya) in the 1950s, supporting the building of new roads and improvement of basic services, providing grants for poverty alleviation and rural development, as well as child and maternal health, and helping to modernise farming methods. Now, this relationship has grown in scope and depth, delivering a wide range of programmes, services and policy advice based on the specialisations and mandates of individual UN Agencies. 
At the same time, Malaysia’s relationship with the UN System continues to grow. For example, Malaysia has attracted the global shared services centres of WHO and UNDP in Cyberjaya and UNU-Administration. These global shared services centres are responsible for the execution and the handling of specific operational tasks, such as accounting, human resources, payroll, IT, legal, compliance, and purchasing for Agency operations around the world. In so doing, they separate these operational tasks from the headquarters of these UN Agencies, which then have more scope to focus on a leadership and corporate governance role.  To service the global operations of these UN Agencies, the centres use the expertise of hundreds of local staff based out of Malaysia, generating employment and broadening opportunities for young Malaysian professionals to gain global experience by working in these international organisations. In all, Malaysia has been found to be an attractive destination for these centres, given its livability and stability.
2.0 Objectives of the UNSDGF 2018-2020
This Framework is therefore aimed at further strengthening the more than half-century of partnership for progress, by addressing the most crucial needs and national priorities for economic and social development as identified in:
The Eleventh Malaysia Plan; 
The 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development and the SDGs, which are further analysed through:
The National SDG Roadmap for Phase 1 (2016-2020)
The Malaysia SDGs Voluntary National Review 2017 
The Regional Roadmap for Implementing the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development in Asia and the Pacific
The country’s performance with respect to the previous Millennium Development Goals (MDGs), at aggregated and disaggregated levels, as of 2015 
The direct voices of Malaysian citizens, as captured in the post-2015 “Malaysia We Want” national dialogues, held in 2014 
The outcomes and recommendations of reviews on Malaysia by international human rights mechanisms, such as the Universal Periodic Review of the Human Rights Council, treaty bodies and special procedures 
The continuous consultative processes of individual UN Agencies in their respective areas of work, prioritisation retreats of the UNCT, and UNCT inputs in the development of Malaysia’s National SDG Roadmap 
The macro-assessment of public financial management, as required under the Harmonised Approach to Cash Transfers (HACT) by UNDP, UNICEF and UNFPA in 2016 
Arising from this, the UNSDGF offers a unified and whole-of-UN System approach to facilitate the kind of integrated technical assistance required to address remaining and emerging challenges, including those that are cross-cutting in nature.   Coordinated UN System support will broaden the options for Government and other partners alike as solutions are sought in key areas to address the complexity and multi-dimensionality involved in driving Malaysia’s development transition. This Framework also formalises the already-close cooperation between the UNCT and Government on the Agenda 2030, and will further focus the joint work of the UN Agencies to help accelerate Malaysia’s attainment of the SDGs for prosperous, inclusive and resilient futures for all.
3.0 The National SDG Roadmap and Country Assessment in Relation to the SDGs
Many reports and analytical documents provide good assessments of the country’s development status and its achievements, as well as its challenges and remaining priorities. These include the MDG Report 2015, the Malaysia SDGs Voluntary National Review 2017 and the Malaysia Human Development Report 2015, among others. All were referred to in the development of this UNSDGF. However, the summary of assessments and priority action areas that follows is based primarily on the National SDG Roadmap 2017, which is Malaysia’s main policy document for SDG implementation, and which forms the rationale for the UNSDGF 2018-2020. 
Malaysia’s SDG Roadmap clusters the 17 Goals of the Agenda 2030 thematically, aligned with key strategic thrusts of the Eleventh Malaysia Plan. Further, it provides in-depth analysis of Malaysia’s current development status, gaps and challenges, as well as the way forward in relation to each SDG under the Roadmap’s five clusters. It also highlights the interlinkages between the various Goals and clusters. Development of the SDG Roadmap thus involved a detailed mapping of the Eleventh Malaysia Plan to the SDGs, its targets and indicators, which was undertaken by the Government’s Economic Planning Unit. The UNCT was substantively involved and provided human and financial resources, to support Malaysia’s development of its National SDG Roadmap for Phase 1. 
3.1 Cluster 1 of the National SDG Roadmap: Inclusivity
The Inclusivity cluster of the National SDG Roadmap, which corresponds to the first strategic thrust of the Eleventh Malaysia Plan on “Enhancing Inclusiveness Toward an Equitable Society,” comprises:
SDG 1: End poverty in all its forms everywhere
SDG 2: End hunger, achieve food security and improved nutrition, and promote sustainable agriculture
SDG 5: Achieve gender equality, and empower all women and girls
SDG 10: Reduce inequality within and among countries
While Malaysia has made substantial progress on all these goals, some key disparities and vulnerabilities persist, especially among rural households, indigenous peoples, youths and children at risk, the urban poor, low-income and female-headed households, the ageing population, the undocumented, and certain vulnerable groups of non-Malaysians within the country’s borders. The SDG Roadmap thereby proposes customised solutions to reduce vulnerabilities, build resilience and address the multiple dimensions of poverty faced by those furthest behind. It also promotes the advancement of the human rights-based approach to development.
The priority action areas for the Inclusivity cluster are as shown above in Figure 1. They include the need for strengthening of social safety nets; addressing remaining data gaps, especially for the poor and vulnerable groups; enhancing food security and resilience  to climate-related natural disasters for small farmers and others involved   in agriculture; the need for robust responses to gender equality and rights, particularly with regard to discrimination and violence against women and children; and partnerships to mainstream gender and to ensure that all vulnerable populations enjoy full protection under the law and are not left behind. In this regard,  efforts will be needed to further analyse the key issues affecting such groups, including non-citizens and refugees.
3.2 Cluster 2 of the National SDG Roadmap: Well-Being
Cluster 2 of the National SDG Roadmap corresponds to the second strategic thrust of the Eleventh Malaysia Plan, “Improving Well-Being for All,” as well as the Eleventh Plan focus on transforming the public service. It comprises the following:
SDG 3: Ensure healthy lives and promote well-being for all at all ages
SDG 11: Make cities and human settlements inclusive, safe, resilient and sustainable
SDG 16: Promote peaceful and inclusive societies for sustainable development, provide access to justice for all, and build effective, accountable and inclusive institutions at all levels
Through its Eleventh Plan, Malaysia takes a balanced and holistic approach to well-being with regard to standard of living and quality of life, and focuses on providing quality health care and affordable housing, as well as social integration toward a united and cohesive country. The assessment of the SDGs under this Cluster reveal changing health care needs according to lifestyle, giving rise to non-communicable diseases, sexual and reproductive health needs, rising care needs for the elderly, and issues of affordability and unserved needs. With more than 70 percent of the population living in urban areas as of 2010, particularly in high-rise, low-income areas, quality of amenities and facilities require strengthening, and data gaps remain for these communities, especially for the Bottom 40% (B40) population, and for those in the informal sector. 
Priority action areas for Cluster 2 are as shown above in Figure 2. These include the need to strengthen institutions, especially those at grassroots level, and for institutions to adopt a more inclusive approach toward the protection of vulnerable groups and in resolving legal identity issues. The SDG Roadmap also highlights local participation and ownership in city-level planning and delivery of services as a key long- term activity. Given the critical nature of SDG16 to all Goals and targets of the SDGs, the SDG Roadmap also points to the need to undertake further studies vis-à-vis this Goal.  
3.3 Cluster 3 of the National SDG Roadmap: Human Capital
The Human Capital cluster of the National SDG Roadmap is linked to the third strategic thrust of the Eleventh Malaysia Plan, “Accelerating Human Capital Development for an Advanced Nation,” and involves the following SDG:
SDG 3: Ensure inclusive and equitable quality education, and promote lifelong learning opportunities for all 
From the SDG perspective, the focus of this cluster would be equitable quality education and lifelong learning opportunities for all, thereby empowering people and transforming lives, communities and societies toward leaving no one behind. 
The emerging challenges through the SDG lens include reaching the remaining pockets of children, albeit a small percentage, who for various socioeconomic or other reasons (e.g., legal status, birth registration issues) may not be enrolling, or who are dropping out before completing their basic or secondary education. They should be identified, and opportunities for holistic second-chance education need to be developed, including for those who complete their final year of secondary education but who do not qualify for a certificate. Skills development in preparation for Industrial Revolution 4.0 also will need to be an important focus moving forward.
The priority action areas for this cluster are as shown in Figure 3. These involve continued efforts for quality education and lifelong education, and strengthening their links to employability; enhanced data and information for monitoring and evaluation; ensuring conducive environments for learning, including for children with special needs; and making Technical and Vocational Education and Training (TVET) an educational pathway of choice. 
3.4 Cluster 4: Environment and Natural Resources
The fourth cluster of the SDG Roadmap, on Environment and Natural Resources, corresponds to the fourth strategic thrust of the Eleventh Malaysia Plan on “Pursuing Green Growth for Sustainability and Resilience” and comprises:
SDG 6: Ensure availability and sustainable management of water and sanitation for all
SDG 7: Ensure access to affordable, reliable, sustainable and modern energy for all
SDG 12: Ensure sustainable consumption and production (SCP) patterns
SDG 13: Take urgent action to combat climate change and its impacts 
SDG 14: Conserve and sustainably use the oceans, seas and marine resources for sustainable development
SDG 15: Protect, restore and promote sustainable use of terrestrial ecosystems, sustainably manage forests, combat desertification, and halt and reverse land degradation and halt biodiversity loss
Green Growth is not just a strategic thrust but, more importantly a “game changer” under the Eleventh Malaysia Plan, with clear strategies to deliver on its sustainability and resilience goals, while also recognising the need to conserve natural endowments for present and future generations. In relation to climate change, the SDG Roadmap highlights, among others, the need to quantify climate change and disaster impacts and to adopt an integrated approach to disaster risk reduction and preparedness. 
The priority action areas under this cluster from an SDG perspective are as shown in Figure 4. They include, among others, better water management and making this issue a federal and state priority; expanding the use of renewable energy and supporting related innovation; making waste management a national priority; accelerating growth of green business; streamlining SCP into the economy and society; and securing long-term sustainability for marine and terrestrial resources, while also correcting activities that adversely impact them.
3.5 Cluster 5: Economic Growth
The fifth cluster under the National SDG Roadmap is linked to the Eleventh Malaysia Plan’s strategic thrust on “Strengthening Infrastructure to Support Economic Expansion” and “Strengthening Economic Growth for Greater Prosperity.” It comprises:
SDG 8: Promote sustained, inclusive and sustainable economic growth, full and productive employment and decent work for all
SDG 9: Build resilient infrastructure, promote inclusive and sustainable industrialisation, and foster innovation
SDG 17: Strengthen the means of implementation and revitalise the global partnership for sustainable development 
Malaysia has been able to sustain economic growth that has been resilient to external shocks and crisis, through prudent macroeconomic management, an open economy, and a strategy for high economic growth with full employment. As a result, the country now is evolving toward green growth and a knowledge- and innovation-based economy. With the SDGs, quality of growth is paramount in terms of inclusivity, equality, resilience and sustainability. Malaysia also has built strong regional and global partnerships and is responding to the increasingly challenging global environment through various bilateral and multilateral fora, particularly in the areas of South-South Cooperation, prevention of violent extremism, disasters and other humanitarian issues. 
The priority action areas under this cluster are shown in Figure 5. They are very much inter-linked with the other clusters, and include diversification of the economy; strengthening governance, including for research and development (R&D); encouraging grassroots innovation; enhancing use of enabling technologies; exploring other South-South Cooperation options; and combating terrorism and fluctuating commodity prices. 
3.6 Key Considerations Moving Forward
The UNCT has been a strong partner of Government on the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development even before the Agenda was globally adopted and supported Malaysia’s preparatory efforts in this regard, as summarised in Figure 6.
The UNCT also is working closely with the Economic Planning Unit on a detailed “way forward” proposal that incorporates, among others, the following key elements identified in the National SDG Roadmap to accelerate Phase 1 implementation and to prepare for Phase 2:
Mainstreaming and localisation of the SDGs, particularly at state levels
Promoting ownership and participation
Mobilisation of resources through partnerships 
Strengthening data readiness and preparations for Phase 2 implementation 
4.0 Alignment of the UNSDGF to Malaysia’s Development Priorities for 2016-2020 and National SDG Roadmap for Phase 1
As highlighted throughout this document, the UNSDGF 2018-2020, through the lens of the National SDG Roadmap, is anchored on the Malaysia’s Eleventh Plan to address remaining issues and spur growth in the crucial years leading up to fulfilment of Vision 2020. It also underscores Malaysia’s aspirations beyond 2020 and its regional and global positions, roles and contributions to development, human rights, peace and security, as well as, most importantly its commitments to delivering on the SDGs by 2030. 
The UNSDGF comes two years after the adoption of the Agenda 2030 and SDGs by the 193 Member States of the United Nations, in September 2015. Malaysia has shown strong commitment to this transformative and ambitious agenda, evidenced in its mainstreaming via the Eleventh Plan and in the inclusive and multi-stakeholder SDG governance structure established in 2016. This governance structure is led by the Prime Minister at the SDG Council level, with the Economic Planning Unit, under the Prime Minister’s Department, as the coordinating body and main focal point for SDG implementation and reporting in the country. The UNCT has been actively engaged through this national mechanism and provided support to development of Malaysia’s National Voluntary Review at the 2017 High-Level Political Forum and Malaysia’s National SDG Roadmap for Phase 1 (2016-2020), both of which highlight the nation’s priorities, challenges and way forward to meet Malaysia’s commitments on the SDGs. The UNCT will continue to work closely with Government and other stakeholders in building awareness, localisation, implementation, monitoring, evaluation and reporting on the SDGs, including the provision of support for systems and capacities in data and statistical analysis. 
As described in Section 3, all 17 SDGs were thematically organised in the National SDG Roadmap for Phase 1 into five clusters (i.e., Inclusivity, Wellbeing; Human Capital; Environment and Natural Resources; and Economic Growth). These were based on the strategic thrusts of the Eleventh Malaysia Plan, which aim to enhance inclusiveness towards an equitable society, improve well-being for all, accelerate human capital development for an advanced nation, pursue green growth for sustainability and resilience, strengthen infrastructure to support economic expansion, re-engineer economic growth for greater prosperity, and humanise public services and reinforce governance. The Eleventh Malaysia Plan also aims to capture the aspirations of the citizenry beyond 2020 across the dimensions of people, economy and environment. These are being further crystalised via the ongoing Transformasi Nasional 2050 (TN50) initiative, to plan for Malaysia’s future for the next 30-year period from 2020 to 2050. 
Development of the outcome areas under the UNSDGF 2018-2020 were therefore guided by the National SDG Roadmap, its clusters and key considerations moving forward, considering the work and mandate of individual UN Agencies as well the synergies between them. As highlighted above, the National SDG Roadmap is therefore a key guidance document to the collective work of the UNCT, as mutually agreed upon with Government via this UNSDGF. 
5.0 Outcome Areas of UNSDGF 2018-2020 
The four results areas of UN cooperation (for joint work of the Agencies) identified under the Framework are:
Outcome Area 1:	Effective Mainstreaming, Localisation, Monitoring Toward Achievement of the SDGs
Outcome Area 1 corresponds to the key considerations moving forward as per the National SDG Roadmap, as described in Section 3.6, as well as to the UNCT’s more detailed “way forward” proposal that has been presented to the Economic Planning Unit. This outcome area also includes part of Cluster 3 on Well-Being under the National SDG Roadmap, which relates to SDG17 and partnerships for development, both in the country and at regional and global levels. 
Description:
The UN System will work closely with the Government, civil society, private sector and other stakeholders to enhance awareness, ownership and multi-stakeholder partnerships on the SDGs at federal and state levels. The outputs will include, among others, (1) the development of subnational SDG Roadmaps; (2) SDG acceleration frameworks and/or catalytic action plans with links to budgeting and financing mechanisms; (3) a monitoring and evaluation framework; (4) complementary tools, including a National SDG Portal and SDG Data Monitoring Dashboard linked to the SDG targets and global indicator framework, which will facilitate statistical analysis; and (5) development of a national SDG report by 2019 to help shape the TN50 approach and the Twelfth Malaysia Plan as a robust Phase 2 SDG implementation framework for 2021-2025.  
The UNCT will support institutional strengthening for quality, timely and reliable disaggregated data availability and analysis, which will be needed to measure progress and to ensure that no one is left behind. This also is key to decision making at all levels, and for monitoring and evaluation purposes. The UNCT will support bringing together key stakeholders and experts in the field, share technology and innovations, and bring in new sources for capacity development. Similarly, an integrated approach to monitoring and evaluation will be supported. The UNCT will continue supporting the evaluation function through the national evaluation capacity development initiative.
The UNCT also will support the sharing and showcasing of Malaysia’s best practices in relation to the Agenda 2030 and SDGs in regional and international platforms. Further, it will encourage Malaysia’s enhanced participation and contribution to South-South and Triangular Cooperation, the global partnership for development in line with SDG 17, the Regional Asia-Pacific 2030 Agenda Roadmap, the High-level Political Forum on Sustainable Development, ASEAN-UN cooperation, and various other bilateral and multilateral fora, taking into account national capacities. Participation in such platforms for cooperation are key to the comprehensive achievement of the ambitious and interconnected goals and targets of the Agenda 2030 to address transboundary challenges through capacity building, knowledge sharing and technical cooperation on the SDGs as well as broader peace and security.
Outcome Area 2:	Enhanced Inclusivity, Empowerment of Women and Improved Well-Being for All Toward Leaving No One Behind (LNOB)
Outcome Area 2 is directly linked to Cluster 1 on Inclusivity, Cluster 2 on Well- Being and Cluster 3 on Human Capital of the National SDG Roadmap, which are mentioned under Sections 3.1, 3.2 and 3.3 above. 
Description:
The principle of leaving no one behind (LNOB) – and, in that context, reaching those furthest behind first – is the overarching principle of the Agenda 2030 and SDGs, and thereby a key commitment of the Government and the mandates of all UN Agencies, Funds and Programmes.  Vulnerable groups in relation to poverty risk, particularly multidimensional poverty, have been identified in the National SDG Roadmap and are summarised in Figure 8.
This area of work will include UN System support for the development and implementation of effective policies and initiatives that integrate the social (LNOB), economic and environmental dimensions for eradicating poverty and deprivation in all their forms;  reducing inequality, and particularly increasing inclusivity and resilience of the bottom 40 percent; ensuring gender equality, reducing gender-based violence and discrimination, and empowering women and girls;  and improving delivery of basic services, including universal health coverage, especially for vulnerable groups such as those living in remote areas, indigenous peoples, the urban poor, persons with disabilities, women, children, youth, the ageing population, and those living with HIV and AIDS.  This also will be supported through research and evidence generation and data strengthening to address the gaps.
This outcome area likewise will include addressing issues relating to human trafficking, forced labour, child labour and non-citizens in vulnerable situations (e.g., the stateless, undocumented, migrants, victims of human trafficking, refugees) within the borders of the country. Such initiatives will range from a focus on well-being to registration (e.g., birth registration, work permits) and employment, with a special focus on the needs of women and children. In this regard, national laws and policies, as well as international standards, laws and conventions to which Malaysia is a signatory along with Malaysia’s registered reservations to these Conventions, all will be taken into account.
Related to this, Malaysia has not yet signed the Convention on Refugees. Nonetheless, Malaysia is making efforts, such as through the UNHCR-Government Joint Task Force, to manage the situation relating to refugees in the country. Further deepening of this collaboration will be important to build on these common efforts to regularise the situation of refugees through initiatives such as registration and employment.
Overall, this outcome area is aligned to the Eleventh Malaysia Plan Strategic Thrust 1 on “Enhancing Inclusiveness Toward an Equitable Society” and Strategic Thrust 2 on “Improving Well-Being for All.” Strategic Thrust 1 focuses on, among others, the middle and bottom 40 percent income group, as well as on community development for women, families, youth, and persons with disabilities, including children. At the same time, Strategic Thrust 2 aims to improve well-being for all Malaysians, regardless of socioeconomic background or geographic location, in terms of equitable access to quality health care, education and affordable housing, as well as to safer neighbourhoods and public spaces, and to strengthen social cohesion and national unity. 
Poverty rates in Malaysia in 2014 stood at less than 0.6 percent overall; in urban and rural areas, these have decreased to 0.3 percent and 1.6 percent respectively since2012. Poverty incidence among all ethnic groups also has improved.9 Despite Malaysia’s remarkable success in reducing poverty at the national and subnational levels, however, persistent pockets of poverty remain, as do gaps within and across states and among vulnerable groups. For example, the incidence of poverty among indigenous peoples in Sabah is as high as 20 percent, whereas for those in Sarawak it is 7 percent. The Orang Asli in Peninsular Malaysia have been identified as among Malaysia’s poorest people. 
Given Malaysia’s advanced stage of development, relative poverty measurements are of great importance. In this regard, the B40 group is highly vulnerable to shocks, increased costs of living and rising household debts. In terms of income inequality, Malaysia’s Gini coefficient has fallen from 0.46 in 2002 to 0.401 in 2014, indicating some improvement. The OECD Economic Assessment on Malaysia, in November 2016, posits that Malaysia’s efforts to further improve relative inequality for individual and societal well-being would require reforms with respect to access to quality education, social protection, labour force participation of women and older persons, health care, pension adequacy and the inclusiveness of the tax and transfer system.
Figures for 2016 show Malaysia’s low unemployment rates, at 3.4 percent, with a labour force participation rate of 67.7 percent; at the same time, some 45.2 percent remain outside the labour force due to schooling and further studies. Unemployment rates for youth aged 15-19, 20-24 and 25-29 were 15.9 percent, 9.1 percent and 4.2 percent respectively for the same year. Critically, male labour force participation is 80.2 percent compared to female labour force participation of 54.3 percent. At the same time, Malaysia’s performance on the Global Gender Gap Index fell to 106th out of 144 countries in 2016, from 102nd out of 136 countries in 2013; the country ranks 134th in terms of women’s political empowerment. 
Malaysia is reportedly home to an estimated 6.7 million foreign workers, out of which only 2.1 million have valid work permits (2014 data). About 150,000 refugees and asylum seekers also are found in the country, according to UNHCR. 
Broadly, Malaysia also is faced with the challenge of making use of its demographic window of opportunity. Data reveal that the number of children will decline by 2050 (from 9.056 million in 2017 to 8.34 million in 2050). Most observers believe the demographic window of opportunity will actually end by 2020. This necessitates the right policy decisions now in order to strengthen the social protection floor and the coping mechanism and resilience of families; strengthening and coordinating social protection coverage for vulnerable groups, including workers in the informal sector, requires particular attention.
Meanwhile, those living on the margins of development still lack access to basic services such as electricity, clean drinking water, appropriate modes of public transportation, good schools and quality education, medical services, and mobile and digital connectivity. To join other countries in the “very high human development” category, Malaysia thus will need to ensure social inclusiveness and equitable opportunities and outcomes, and to narrow remaining income gaps. 
Outcome Area 3:	Inclusive Governance and Human Rights for All
Outcome Area 3 relates to the National SDG Roadmap’s Cluster 3 on Well-Being, which includes SDG16, and to the Eleventh Malaysia Plan focus on governance, institutions and transforming the public service for productivity. 
Description:
The collective efforts of the UNCT under this outcome area will focus on the pillars of good governance, access to justice (including justice for children), institutional development, and human rights at national and subnational levels. The combined focus under this broad outcome area is derived from the scope of the targets and indicators under SDG16, which encompass peace, justice, good governance, participation, human rights and institutional development, all of which are crucial for the successful implementation of the 2030 Agenda and SDGs. Malaysia also is a signatory to the United Nations Convention Against Corruption, with transformation of the public service a key priority under the Eleventh Malaysia Plan. Hence, the aim will be to support Government efforts toward ensuring that Malaysia’s system of governance and public accountability meets the country’s regional and international commitments and achieves international standards.
The elements of governance and human rights also are enshrined in the ASEAN Community Vision 2025, adopted under the Kuala Lumpur Declaration on ASEAN 2025: Forging Ahead Together. Article A.2 of the Declaration states the commitment of ASEAN Member States to “strengthen democracy, good governance, the rule of law, promotion and protection of human rights and fundamental freedoms, as well as combat corruption.”
Under this outcome area, the UNCT also will support Malaysia’s efforts in the promotion and protection of human rights, including through adherence to the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, ratification of core international human rights Conventions, greater engagement with UN human rights mechanisms, and addressing of recommendations arising from these mechanisms (e.g., Universal Periodic Review, treaty bodies and missions of UN Special Rapporteurs). At the same time, Malaysia’s Constitution, national laws and policies would be respected. Priority focus also would be given to Malaysia’s obligations under core international human rights Conventions to which it is a signatory, including the Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination Against Women (CEDAW), Convention on the Rights of the Child (CRC), Convention of the Rights of Persons with Disabilities (CRPD), and Fundamental Conventions on Forced Labour, Child Labour, Equal Remuneration, and Rights to Organize and Collective Bargaining.
In relation to governance, Malaysia aims to reach the 30th percentile   among developed countries in Transparency International’s annual Corruption Perceptions Index by 2020, on which it currently ranks 55th out of 176 countries. At the same time, elements of good governance such as effectiveness, transparency and accountability apply to both Government and non-Government organisations.  Areas that could be further enhanced include the dissemination and accessibility of information and data at all levels including for those in rural areas with limited connectivity; the independence of key institutions; strengthened inter-Ministerial and inter-institutional coordination for policymaking and enhanced service delivery; and a more participatory system of governance. 
Outcome Area 4:	 Sustainable Economic Development, Prioritising Protection of the Environment and Natural Resources Management
Outcome Area 4 corresponds to the National SDG Roadmap’s Cluster 4 on Environment and Natural Resources and Cluster 5 on Economic Growth. 
Description:
Sustainability underpins all of the SDGs and has tradeoffs and synergies across the Goals and targets. It requires not only the Government to legislate and incentivise change, but also the private sector and other stakeholders to carry out their responsibilities in adopting and internalising sustainable practices in business activities and operations as well as in daily life. The UN System will promote sustainability principles, such as sustainable production and consumption and eco-efficiency, in policy formulation and systems across various levels of Government (federal, state, local)  in order to enhance resilience and increase policy coherence and coordination.  Areas of interest will include interlinking policy on cross-sectoral climate change mitigation and adaptation measures, such as low-carbon cities, energy efficiency in building and industrial sectors, and management of waste and chemical sectors, with a focus on people-centric development. 
Innovative research and pilot projects on biodiversity conservation, ensuring natural resources security and enhancing alternative livelihoods for indigenous and local communities will be explored. Eco-tourism and ecosystem-based management will be a growth sector to be promoted, thereby placing traditional and ecological knowledge at the centre with a view to receiving fair returns for future use and access.
The UN System’s advisory services and technical assistance also will focus on issues related to land use, deforestation and land degradation, which exacerbate disasters such as flood and landslides.  Such assistance likewise will recommend mainstreaming disaster risk reduction and strengthening multi-hazard risk governance, climate adaptability and risk management policy options for lowering risks posed by extreme weather events, especially for low-income households and vulnerable communities.  The UN System will continue to support Malaysia in meeting its multilateral environmental agreements (e.g., the Paris Climate Agreement), by enhancing its capacity to negotiate and report to the Conventions, mobilising climate finance, and facilitating best practices and lessons learned via South-South Cooperation.
6.0 Comparative Advantages of the UN System 
The UNSDGF 2018-2020 is aimed at facilitating integrated approaches by participating UN Agencies such that Malaysia can meet the requirements of an upper-middle-income country. In so doing, it will support the country to make that leap to developed-nation status in a comparatively short span of time, while also facilitating sustained achievements in an uncertain global context. 
Underpinning this is the UN System’s unique value proposition of having diverse capabilities, expertise, experiences and resources in-country, as well as regionally and globally; its LNOB focus, as reflected in the 2030 Agenda and SDGs; extensive engagement and experience at the community level and with federal and state agencies; and its partnerships with civil society and the private sector. Further, the UN System possesses a strong ability to test models at subnational levels and provide proof of concept for scaling up and accelerated progress. It likewise has unique convening power, founded on impartiality and trust and the ability to create “safe spaces” for dialogue on difficult issues. All this is complemented by its global network, tested solutions, best practices and international standards, as well as by its ability to communicate development change. Critically, the UN  also is able to provide global platforms to showcase Malaysia’s achievements, enable learning opportunities and to provide improved visibility for the country in various sectors. 
Collectively, participating UN Agencies have wide-ranging and substantial combined experience and expertise in development planning and strategy, policy advice, capacity building, stakeholder engagement, evidence and data generation, analysis and assessments. This holds true particularly in the areas of: inclusive and resilient economic and social development; sustainable energy and environmental approaches; good governance and accountability; population dynamics; child well-being and youth engagement; decent work and social protection; health; HIV and AIDS; education and culture; science, technology and innovation; sustainable industrial development; humanitarian response, disaster preparedness and risk reduction; labour and human capital development; gender equality and empowerment; human rights and social justice;  rights of migrants; protection of refugees, and provision of assistance to undocumented and stateless people; and provision of transactional and operational support to global development efforts and programmes. 
Fundamentally, the UN System has the unparalleled added advantage of being able to leverage and integrate the diverse capacities, know-how, experience and resources of its more than 30 Funds, Programmes and specialised Agencies present in almost every part of the world, helping to improve and prosper the lives of people, raise standards of living, find solutions to issues of peace and security, safeguard the dignity and rights of those most at risk, hasten development, and increase resilience of countries and regions. It also is uniquely positioned to bring together various development actors and its 193 Member States on a wide scope of issues, to advocate, and to define new development pathways and goals in the face of emerging trends.
The UN System can further support development priorities in Malaysia by undertaking analysis and assessments; providing policy advice; and building capacity, including by facilitating learning and knowledge sharing of global best practices. It is well- positioned to contribute to enhancing participatory and inclusive policy- and decision-making processes in the country through its horizontal and vertical associations with the various stakeholders of the development process and use of new technologies. The UNCT also is well-represented in the governance structure set up by the Economic Planning Unit for implementation, monitoring, evaluation and reporting on the SDGs; this encompasses the SDG Steering Committee, Cluster Working Committees and Task Forces for each Goal.
Since this is the first coordinated framework of the UN system with the Government of Malaysia, it builds upon the lessons learned by similar frameworks in other jurisdictions, particularly those in middle-income countries. And built into the UNSDGF is a sufficient degree of flexibility and agility, to respond to the evolving needs and priorities of the nation, by maintaining it at an outcome level.
7.0 Programme Management and Accountability Arrangements
Because the UNSDGF 2018-2020 is an outcome-level strategic framework, its operationalisation will be undertaken through the development of a Results Matrix, as highlighted above. This will encompass not only results-focused and risk-informed programming, but also monitoring and evaluation provisions. Again, it is critical to note that implementation arrangements for the UNSDGF will not impinge on existing modalities between individual UN entities and their counterpart Government Ministries and/or agencies. 
However, to ensure mutual ownership, alignment and accountability, the Results Matrix, once developed, will be monitored on a yearly basis and reviewed by a National Steering Committee (NSC), jointly chaired by the authority designated by the Government of Malaysia and the UN Resident Coordinator. Membership of the NSC will be decided jointly by its co-chairs. 
The NSC also will be tasked with ensuring sufficient flexibility and agility of the partnership to enable adaptation and appropriate, timely responses to the evolving development needs and priorities of the nation. This may entail adjusting the outcomes and indicators as required to advance Malaysia’s ambitious development agenda, ensure fulfilment of its international commitments and obligations, and expand its support to development, humanitarian aid and peace and security beyond the country’s borders. 
On the part of the UNCT, inter-Agency groups, including Results Groups corresponding to the outcomes areas of the UNSDGF, are in place, as shown in Diagram 1 below. The SDG Working Group, Results Groups and Gender Theme Group of the UNCT will be tasked with undertaking the planning, programming, analysis and effective implementation of the UNSDGF 2018-2020. They also will be responsible for the reporting, monitoring and review processes as required, under the leadership of the UN Resident Coordinator and UNCT. 
These mechanisms will be supported and coordinated by the Office of the UN Resident Coordinator (RCO) to ensure that annual reports on achievements under this framework are produced for periodic monitoring and review. As indicated above, in keeping with the need for a flexible and agile strategic framework that is responsive to the evolving needs of the nation, the review process will enable revisions and/or changes as may be required and deemed appropriate by the NSC in moving forward. 
Diagram 1: UNCT Inter-Agency Coordination Structure
UNCT: United Nations Country Team; HCT: Humanitarian Country Team; WG: Working Group; GTG: Gender Theme Group; UNCG: UN Communications Group; OMT: Operations Management Team; ENV: Environment; DEV: Development
As shown in the inter-Agency coordination structure of the UNCT, a Humanitarian Country Team (HCT) also is chaired by the UN Resident Coordinator, who is simultaneously the de facto Humanitarian Coordinator. The HCT is comprised of UN Agencies, the National Disaster Management Agency (NADMA) and other humanitarian actors from both non-government organisations and the private sector. It is convened periodically to foster a coordinated approach to disaster risk management, preparedness and response. Further, crisis management, preparedness and response is one the 10 core coordination functions of the RCO; other core functions of this Office include (1) strategic analysis and planning; (2) oversight of the UN Country Programming cycle; (3) representation of and support to the UN Secretariat and UN Agencies, including non-resident Agencies; (4) support to national coordination systems and processes; (5) development and management of shared operational support services; (6) external communication and advocacy; (7) human rights and development; (8) joint resource mobilisation and fund management; and (9) general UNCT oversight and coordination.
